column3: It closely repeats the waiting formula with angels and the Lord, and marks the arrival as a point after which faith cannot avail.
It begins the nearby contrast between persuasive speech and entrenched opposition that leads into the warning of 2:210.
Its closing return of all matters to Allah directly reinforces the final clause of 2:210.
It closely parallels the question of waiting for angels or the Lord's command and frames it as self-wronging.
It supplies the destructive conduct of the nearby opponent, sharpening why the surrounding warning is grave.
Its completed decree shows qada al-amr as an enacted, irreversible conclusion.
It presents waiting only for the Hour to arrive suddenly, closely matching the deferred decisive arrival in 2:210.
It adds the nearby refusal of taqwa through sinful pride and the stated consequence before 2:210.
Its qada al-amr establishes a matter as settled beyond the uncertainty under discussion.
It directly repeats that all matters return to Allah, while grounding that return in His dominion.
It completes the nearby contrast by showing self-giving for Allah's pleasure rather than the preceding corrupt conduct.
Its extended shade shares only the surface imagery of zulal, without the cloud, arrival, or decree of 2:210.
It joins Allah's execution of a matter already to be done with the return of matters to Him.
As the immediate preceding command, it identifies the demanded response whose abandonment makes 2:210's warning pertinent.
The contrast of shade and heat shares only the word field of zulal and adds little to the scene in 2:210.
It directly repeats the return of matters to Allah and adds His knowledge of what lies before and behind.
The immediate warning after clear proofs provides the condition to which 2:210 responds with its decisive question.
It presents death followed by return to the Lord, supporting the final return in 2:210.
It places angels around the Throne with judgment rendered in truth, illuminating the angelic and decretive scene.
It immediately follows by recalling clear signs and warning against replacing Allah's favor, extending the admonition.
Its challenge to let opponents settle their affair without delay supplies a limited contrast to awaiting Allah's settlement.
It explicitly links the requested descent of an angel to the decree being settled and the end of respite.
It continues the nearby sequence by relocating present mockery within the Day of Resurrection.
Its cloud covering is a concrete Qur'anic use of al-ghamam, though here it is provision rather than judgment.
It repeats the return of matters to Allah in the context of rejected messengers, but adds no arrival scene.
It follows the passage by presenting revelation as the means for judging human disagreement after clear proofs.
Its repeated return into punishment has no close link to the waiting, clouds, angels, or decree in 2:210.
Its overlapping layers of fire give zulal a threatening sense, unlike the cloud scene but relevant to warning.
It continues the local progression from trial and delayed help to confidence that Allah's help is near.
It associates a day of al-zullah with a great punishment, giving a punitive precedent for overhead covering imagery.
It states that Allah governs al-amr, directly supporting the attribution of the settled matter in 2:210.
Its directed charity instruction belongs to the adjacent passage but adds little to the decisive arrival in 2:210.
Its denial of return to Allah supplies the opposite stance to the final return asserted in 2:210.
Its pleasant shade shares an image word but not the judgment, angels, or return of 2:210.
Its contrast between human preference and Allah's knowledge is nearby but only indirectly related to the warning.
The inability of the calf to answer or control harm and benefit does not materially clarify 2:210.
Mention of angels in a curse context does not illuminate their role in the arrival scene of 2:210.
It develops the nearby stakes of turning back from the religion and the lasting consequence in the Fire.
Its confession of belonging to Allah and returning to Him supports the final return of matters in 2:210.
It explicitly joins a sky split with al-ghamam and the descending angels, closely illuminating the visual scene.
It completes the local contrast with believers who act, migrate, and strive while hoping for Allah's mercy.
It combines Allah's judgment with return to Him, directly reinforcing the closure of 2:210.
Its shade for the muttaqun is only a distant lexical counterpart to the clouds and decree of 2:210.
Its call to reflect on clarified signs is locally adjacent but does not clarify the arrival or decree.
Its commanded movement toward a three-branched shade shares only a remote image word.
It places angels in worship above the earth, providing limited context for their presence in 2:210.
Its distinction between corrupter and reformer is adjacent but does not add to the decisive scene.
It states that Allah gives life and death and that people return to Him, supporting the final return.
Its cloud covering and response of self-wronging parallel elements of 2:210, though its setting is provision.
It depicts wrongdoers standing before their Lord and exchanging blame, a later consequence consistent with return.
Angels' fear and the thunderbolt warning provide only a broad atmosphere of divine power.
Allah's inheritance of earth and those on it, followed by return to Him, reinforces ultimate disposition.
It warns plotters that punishment may come from where they do not perceive, echoing unexpected arrival.
It links worship of the Creator with return to Him, supporting the final orientation of 2:210.
Its waiting for realization and the later wish to be returned to act differently strongly clarifies a too-late decisive arrival.
Inability to go forward or return after transformation does not clarify the divine arrival or decree in 2:210.
It states that people are held from faith until the precedent of earlier peoples or punishment comes before them.
Its return to Hell supplies a specific punitive destination, while 2:210 states the more general return of matters.
Angelic prostration establishes submission but does not clarify the scene, decree, or return in 2:210.
It directly states return to Allah and His power over all things, supporting the final clause.
Its declaration that the whole matter belongs to Allah directly supports the ownership of al-amr in 2:210.
Allah's power to restore supports the possibility implied by the final return, but lacks the scene's other features.
Mocking each prophet gives a broad rejection pattern but no close link to the wording or structure of 2:210.
Completion of a contractual term uses qada in a distinct, non-eschatological setting.
Its repeated mockery of messengers is only a general rejection parallel.
Creation, restoration, and return to Allah reinforce the ultimate return announced in 2:210.
Its mention of angels and the Last Day is part of a broad ethical definition, with little direct explanatory value.
Completion of Moses' term followed by travel and fire has no close relation to the decisive arrival in 2:210.
Turning away whenever a renewed reminder comes supplies a rejection pattern relevant to waiting after signs.
It states the return to Allah and disclosure of deeds, supporting accountability at the return.
It depicts the record, prophets, witnesses, and judgment in truth, closely explaining the settled affair of 2:210.
Expectation of meeting the Lord and returning to Him supports the final return in 2:210.
It begins after the matter has been settled and exposes the failure of false promises at that final point.
Its legal limits and possible return within marriage do not materially clarify 2:210.
It places regret at the sight of punishment with judgment in equity, closely illuminating the final decree.
It rejects the idea that people are not to be returned to Allah, directly supporting the final return.
Its divine decree is a command of worship and kindness, not the settling of the affair in 2:210.
Its shade of black smoke gives a threatening counter-image for overhead covering, though not al-ghamam.
It closely repeats waiting only for the Hour to come suddenly and stresses the futility of reminder once it arrives.
Its sequence of life, death, renewed life, and return to Allah supports the final return.
It portrays the Spirit and angels standing in ranks on a day of restricted speech, furnishing judgment-day context for the angels.
Its wish for a death that would have been decisive highlights the irreversible finality associated with qada al-amr.
Allah alone begins and repeats creation, supporting His exclusive authority over return and final outcomes.
It explicitly joins return to Allah with full recompense and no injustice, clarifying the accountability of return.
It states that the entire matter belongs to Allah and that His promise will come, supporting divine control and arrival.
The messenger's return to people with an interpretation does not materially illuminate 2:210.
It depicts humbled, furtive looking before enduring punishment, a consequence compatible with the warned arrival.
Its return to the city is a political claim, not the return to Allah or the decisive scene of 2:210.
The challenge concerning Allah's help and private scheming does not clarify the wording or logic of 2:210.
It states the collective return to Allah and disclosure of deeds, supporting the accountability implied by 2:210.
Its description of rushing into sin does not add to the arrival, angels, decree, or return in 2:210.
The messenger's return to the king is unrelated to the return of matters to Allah in 2:210.
It gathers Allah's enemies toward the Fire, supplying a concrete consequence of the final summons.
It explicitly says that the matter would be settled between the parties and reserves knowledge of wrongdoers to Allah.
Its abasement and wrath concern a distinct historical judgment and add little to 2:210.
It explicitly says a prior word to an appointed term prevents the matter from being settled prematurely.
Its inheritance allocations do not clarify the scene or conclusion of 2:210.
Its command to return from a house is a distinct social instruction, not a theological return.
Its appointed debt term is a distant temporal parallel without explanatory value for 2:210.
The command to return to the Lord supports the personal dimension of the final return in 2:210.
The demand to see Allah openly supplies a relevant earlier form of seeking an overwhelming divine manifestation.
It states that all in the heavens and earth submit willingly or unwillingly and are returned to Allah.
It affirms that Allah will gather people for the Day of Resurrection, supporting the final return and reckoning.
It joins Allah's dominion over heavens and earth with the destination to Him.
Even the descent of angels and every sign would not compel faith without Allah's will, qualifying demands for visible proof.
It says the Hour comes suddenly and asks about its appointed time, closely matching the waiting and arrival in 2:210.
It portrays Allah's command arriving by night or day and reducing apparent worldly security to aftermath.
It says the command of the Lord has come and an unreturnable punishment is coming, sharpening irrevocability.
It declares Allah predominant over His affair, directly supporting the divine ownership and settlement of al-amr.
It states that Allah directs the affair, reinforcing the attribution of al-amr in 2:210.
It links the descent of angels in truth with the end of granted delay, closely explaining the angelic arrival.
It announces that Allah's command has come and forbids haste, strongly paralleling the awaited decisive command.
It portrays angels descending by Allah's command, directly relevant to their presence in 2:210.
It likens the affair of the Hour to a blink or nearer, supporting the abruptness of the decisive arrival.
It names a Day of Regret when the matter has been settled while people had been heedless.
It announces the nearness of people's reckoning while they remain heedlessly turned away.
It says the awaited event comes suddenly, confounds them, and cannot be repelled or deferred.
It says disbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour comes suddenly or the punishment of a barren day comes.
It makes the day of seeing angels a day without good news for the guilty, closely relevant to the angels of 2:210.
It assigns dominion on that Day to the Most Merciful and calls it hard for disbelievers.
It portrays the Trumpet day and universal fear before Allah, furnishing final-day context for the scene.
Hope of meeting Allah and the certainty of His term support the horizon of return and judgment.
It states that every soul tastes death and is then returned to Allah.
Knowledge of the Hour belongs to Allah, supporting the hidden timing of the awaited event.
It states that Allah directs the affair from above the heavens, supporting His disposal of al-amr.
It describes the affair descending from heaven and then ascending to Him, further framing divine governance of al-amr.
It says the Hour may be near, contributing the imminence of the event awaited in 2:210.
It says they await only one blast that seizes them while they dispute, a close sudden-arrival parallel.
It depicts the Trumpet followed by emergence from graves and hastening toward the Lord.
It reduces the event to one blast after which all are brought before Allah.
It presents the Trumpet, death, renewed rising, and standing in expectation before Allah.
It depicts the Day when all are exposed and exclusive sovereignty belongs to Allah.
It states that the Hour is certainly coming although most people do not believe.
It says faith did not benefit people once they saw Allah's might, closely matching the too-late logic of 2:210.
It reserves knowledge of the Hour to Allah and describes people questioning its arrival.
It states that the Hour may be near after mentioning the Book and the balance sent down in truth.
It commands response before an irreversible Day from Allah arrives, closely clarifying the warning's urgency.
It identifies the matter as knowledge or a sign of the Hour and prohibits doubt concerning it.
It calls for watching the day when the sky brings a visible smoke, a related overhead eschatological image.
It says that to Allah all are returned after linking each soul to its own deeds.
It depicts angels taking disbelievers at death while striking their faces and backs, showing an angelic judgment encounter.
It portrays the blast arriving with truth as the Day of the threatened reality.
It depicts every soul arriving with a driver and a witness, supplying a concrete final-account scene.
It announces that the Hour has drawn near, directly supporting the imminence of 2:210's awaited event.
It identifies the Hour as the appointed time and calls it more grievous and bitter.
It announces the occurrence of the inevitable event, supporting the certainty of the final scene.
It states that death is unavoidable and that people are then returned to the Knower of unseen and seen.
It rejects denial of resurrection and affirms return to Allah as certain and within His power.
It names the Day of Gathering as the day of mutual loss and gain, adding final-day context.
It describes Allah's command descending among the heavens and earth, supporting His active disposal of al-amr.
It describes angels as stern and unwavering in executing Allah's commands, relevant to their judicial presence.
It preserves the challenge about when the promise will come, echoing the waiting posture of 2:210.
It reserves knowledge of the promised time to Allah and defines the messenger as a clear warner.
It opens the final catastrophe with the single blast of the Trumpet.
It portrays the Day of presentation when no secret remains hidden.
It depicts rapid emergence from graves toward erected markers, as though hurrying to a summoned point.
It presents faces on that Day looking toward their Lord, a direct visual counterpart to the divine-presence language.
It culminates the dying sequence with being driven to the Lord on that Day.
It designates the Day of Decision as a fixed appointment, directly relevant to final settlement.
It describes the Hereafter's day as seeming only an evening or its morning to those who see it.
Its unfolding cosmic signs introduce the Day when every soul knows what it has brought.
Its cosmic rupture sequence leads to each soul knowing what it sent ahead and left behind.
Its cosmic transformation ends with humanity meeting its Lord.
Its earth-shaking and disclosure of burdens culminate in people seeing the outcome of their deeds.
It names the striking calamity and asks what can convey its reality, giving a concentrated final-day parallel.
